The nestling stage of the Spotted flycatcher (Muscicapa striata) begins with the moment of hatching, following an incubation period that typically lasts just under two weeks. Field studies have measured the age at hatching as approximately 13.5 days [ab = approximately 13.5 days] when eggs are incubated at a constant temperature of 32 °C [T = 32 °C], reflecting the thermal conditions that optimize embryonic development. The newly hatched chick is extraordinarily small, with an initial wet body mass of only 1.92 grams [Ww0 = 1.92 grams], a value that underscores the altricial nature of this passerine. This modest birth mass demands intensive parental provisioning from both the male and female, who must forage continuously to meet the energetic needs of the rapidly developing brood. The nestling period is comparatively brief, and the young birds progress quickly through feather development and wing muscle growth before they are ready to leave the nest for the first time.

By the time the chicks fledge, they have undergone a remarkable transformation in both size and physiological capacity. Fledging, marking the achievement of first flight and nest departure, occurs 15 days after birth [tx = 15 days after birth] under the active metabolic conditions typical of the breeding season, when ambient temperatures approximate 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. At this stage, the fledgling weighs considerably more than its hatchling mass, though it has not yet attained the full adult body size. The period following fledging is a critical phase of skill acquisition, during which the young bird learns to hunt flying insects independently while still receiving occasional food from its parents. This developmental milestone sets the stage for the next major life-history transition, which involves the attainment of reproductive capability after several more weeks of growth and maturation.

Sexual maturation in the Spotted flycatcher proceeds steadily after fledging, culminating in the onset of gonadal activity. The time since birth at puberty has been calculated at 45 days [tp = 45 days] when birds are maintained at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a value indicative of the species' relatively rapid sexual development compared to some other temperate passerines. Following the achievement of puberty, there is often a considerable delay before the individual engages in its first breeding attempt. The time since birth at first brood has been documented at 365 days [tR = 365 days] under the same thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], suggesting that young flycatchers typically defer reproduction until their second calendar year, a pattern that may be linked to the energetic demands of establishing a territory and acquiring sufficient foraging experience.

The ultimate body mass achieved by adult Spotted flycatchers exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females attaining a significantly larger size than males. The ultimate wet weight for females reaches approximately 18.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 18.5 grams], while the ultimate wet weight for males is notably lower at 15.2 grams [Wwi = 15.2 grams]. This difference in adult body mass likely reflects divergent selective pressures acting on the two sexes, with the larger female possibly benefiting from enhanced fecundity or improved thermoregulation during incubation. The life span of this species, when considered under optimal conditions at a metabolic temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], has been estimated at roughly 8.7 years [am = roughly 8.7 years] based on the oldest documented individuals in banding studies. This relatively modest longevity is consistent with the species' position in the fast-slow continuum of life-history strategies among small insectivorous passerines.

Reproductive output in the Spotted flycatcher is characterized by a moderate clutch size and a restricted breeding season. Females typically lay between 3 and 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 3 and 4 eggs per clutch] and may produce approximately 1 to 2 clutches annually [F_R_i = approximately 1 to 2 clutches annually] under favorable conditions when ambient temperatures reach 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The daily maintenance costs incurred by an actively foraging adult are reflected in its basal metabolic rate, which has been measured at 44.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 44.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when the bird is at rest at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively high metabolic demand, combined with the energetic investment required to provision a brood of rapidly growing nestlings, explains why the species often limits itself to a single clutch in years of poor food abundance. The interplay between metabolic physiology and reproductive scheduling highlights the finely tuned life-history strategy of this aerial insectivore.
